(CNN) — A Marine accused of killing Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach, who was more than eight months pregnant at the time of her death, was not the father of her unborn child, a law enforcement source close to the murder investigation said Saturday.

Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean, who is being held on a murder charge, is scheduled to be arraigned in June. According to the source, who has reviewed a report completed earlier this month by the Defense Department’s Armed Forces Institute of Pathology, Laurean’s DNA does not match that of Lauterbach’s unborn child, who also died.

Laurean and Lauterbach were both stationed at Camp Lejeune in North Carolina. An autopsy determined that Lauterbach, 20, died from blunt force trauma to the head. In January 2008, police unearthed her charred body from beneath a barbecue pit in Laurean’s backyard. She had disappeared the previous month.

Laurean was 22 when he was arrested in Mexico in April 2008. At the time, a Mexican reporter asked him whether he had killed Lauterbach. The Marine replied, “I loved her.”

Laurean has been indicted on charges including first-degree murder, financial card transaction fraud, and obtaining property by false pretenses. North Carolina prosecutors allege that he killed Lauterbach on December 14 and used her ATM card 10 days later before fleeing to Mexico. He holds dual citizenship in the United States and Mexico.

The law enforcement source familiar with the case said a DNA swab was taken from Laurean by court order after he was extradited from Mexico in March to face charges in North Carolina. Mexican authorities agreed to the extradition in part because prosecutors removed the possibility of the death penalty. Mexico does not have the death penalty.

Before her death, Lauterbach told the Marines that Laurean had raped her. The month before she disappeared, Lauterbach’s mother said Maria told a military investigator that she no longer believed Laurean was the father of her unborn child. However, her mother, Mary Lauterbach, said her daughter remained adamant that Laurean had raped her. Laurean denied the allegation.

A few weeks before a scheduled rape hearing at Camp Lejeune, Lauterbach disappeared.

Dewey Hudson, district attorney for Onslow County, said Laurean is scheduled for arraignment in early June and is expected to enter a plea. “I cannot comment on any of the tests,” Hudson said. He declined to say how the DNA results might affect the case against Laurean.

Through her attorney, Mary Lauterbach said the DNA test results do not answer broader questions about whether the Marines did enough to protect her daughter or acted quickly enough in investigating her claims.

“We do not believe that the result will have any effect on the continuing investigation or the trial,” said Lauterbach’s attorney, Merle Wilberding.

**ONSLOW COUNTY, N.C. —** Former Marine Cpl. Cesar Armando Laurean has been extradited from Mexico to North Carolina to face charges in the killing of Marine Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach, a pregnant 20-year-old service member whose death drew national attention after her remains were discovered buried in a fire pit behind Laurean’s home.

Laurean, who had been stationed with Lauterbach at Camp Lejeune, was arrested in Mexico after fleeing the United States in January 2008, shortly before investigators found Lauterbach’s body. Mexican authorities captured him in Michoacán, and after a lengthy extradition process, he was returned to North Carolina under an agreement that prosecutors would not seek the death penalty, a condition commonly required by Mexico in extradition cases.

Laurean is expected to appear in Onslow County Superior Court for arraignment on charges tied to Lauterbach’s death. He faces a first-degree murder charge, along with additional counts related to the alleged theft and use of Lauterbach’s bank card and other property.

### Discovery of Lauterbach’s Body

Lauterbach disappeared in December 2007 while about eight months pregnant. Her family reported her missing after she failed to return home to Ohio for the holidays. Investigators later focused on Laurean, who lived in Jacksonville, North Carolina, near Camp Lejeune.

In January 2008, authorities found charred human remains in a shallow grave and fire pit in Laurean’s backyard. The remains were identified as Lauterbach’s, and investigators said evidence indicated she had been killed before her body was burned and buried.

An autopsy determined that Lauterbach died from blunt-force trauma to the head. Her unborn child also died. Prosecutors have alleged that Laurean killed Lauterbach and attempted to conceal the crime by burning her remains.

### DNA Test Results

DNA testing became a significant element of the investigation because Lauterbach had accused Laurean of raping her months before her death and was pregnant at the time she disappeared.

Authorities later reported that DNA testing showed Laurean was **not** the father of Lauterbach’s unborn child. The results were important because they undercut speculation that the pregnancy itself was evidence of Laurean’s alleged sexual assault, though investigators continued to examine the broader circumstances surrounding Lauterbach’s rape allegation and her later killing.

### Rape Allegations Against Laurean

Before her death, Lauterbach had accused Laurean of sexually assaulting her in 2007 while both were serving in the Marine Corps. The allegation was under investigation by military authorities, and Lauterbach was expected to testify in connection with the case.

Laurean denied the rape allegation. At the time of Lauterbach’s disappearance and death, the sexual assault investigation had not resulted in a conviction. Prosecutors have not described the rape allegation as proven, but it remains a central part of the background of the case because it connected Lauterbach and Laurean before the murder and raised questions about motive.

### Flight to Mexico and Extradition

After investigators began questioning Laurean, he fled North Carolina and crossed into Mexico. His wife reportedly provided authorities with a note in which Laurean claimed Lauterbach had killed herself and that he had buried her body out of panic. Investigators rejected that account, citing physical evidence and the condition of the remains.

Laurean’s arrest in Mexico triggered a prolonged extradition process. Because Mexico does not extradite suspects who may face capital punishment, North Carolina prosecutors agreed not to pursue the death penalty. That cleared the way for Laurean’s transfer back to the United States to stand trial.

### Upcoming Court Proceedings

At his upcoming arraignment in Onslow County, Laurean is expected to be formally advised of the charges against him and asked to enter a plea. Prosecutors are preparing to move forward with the murder case now that he is back in North Carolina custody.

The case remains one of the most closely watched criminal proceedings involving Camp Lejeune personnel, combining allegations of sexual assault, a missing pregnant Marine, an international manhunt, and a murder prosecution that may hinge on forensic evidence and witness testimony.
